lesson.title: Trusting the Numbers: How Instruments Get Calibrated
lesson.summary: Calibration is the process of checking an instrument's readings against a known, trusted reference and correcting for any drift, which is what gives you a reason to actually believe the numbers a multimeter or oscilloscope displays.
lesson.body:
A multimeter or an oscilloscope reports a number, but that number is only trustworthy if the instrument's internal reference values, its voltage reference, its amplifier gains, its time base oscillator, are themselves accurate. None of these stay perfectly fixed forever. Components age, temperature changes shift resistor and semiconductor behavior slightly, and small internal reference voltages can drift over months and years of use. Calibration is the practice of periodically checking an instrument's readings against a known, trusted reference standard and adjusting the instrument, or at minimum recording how far off it has drifted, so that its readings can still be relied upon.

Oscilloscopes commonly provide a small, practical version of this on the front panel: a calibration terminal that outputs a square wave of a known, fixed frequency, often around 1 kilohertz, and a known amplitude, typically on the order of a few volts. This is not a full calibration of the scope's internal accuracy, it is primarily there so you can check and adjust the compensation of your probe, touching the probe to that terminal and confirming the square wave's corners look sharp and flat on screen rather than rounded or overshooting, which tells you the probe itself is correctly matched to the scope's input. A full calibration, one that actually verifies the accuracy of the vertical amplifier's gain and the time base's timing, requires comparing the instrument against laboratory reference standards with a known, certified accuracy of their own, and is typically performed on a fixed schedule, often annually, by a calibration lab, with a sticker or certificate recording the date it was last done and, often, when it is due again.

A multimeter is checked the same way in spirit: its readings are compared against precision reference sources, a precision voltage reference or a precision resistor of known value, and adjusted or documented accordingly. Between full lab calibrations, a reasonable sanity check is to measure something whose value you already trust, like a fresh battery of a known nominal voltage or a precision resistor, and confirm the meter agrees within its stated accuracy.

The reason any of this matters is straightforward: every measurement you make is only as good as your reason to trust the instrument making it. An oscilloscope that has drifted so its vertical amplifier now reads 3 percent high will make every voltage you measure with it look 3 percent larger than it really is, consistently, on every reading, until it is recalibrated. That kind of consistent, instrument caused offset is exactly the second major source of the systematic error discussed in the next chapter, alongside the loading error covered just before this one.
